messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Leilani was thirty-five years old, a married woman who worked as an accountant in a mid-sized firm downtown. She came to therapy with a PCL-5 score of 71, and she had not slept through the night in over fourteen months. The event that had broken her life open happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, after she had stayed late to close out a quarterly report. She had left the office just after eight, walking the six blocks to the train station as she had done hundreds of times before. She was wearing headphones, listening to a podcast, when she felt a hand close around her upper arm from behind. The grip was hard and sudden, and before she could turn, a man yanked her backward into the narrow alley between two buildings. She dropped her bag. He was wearing a dark hood, and she saw his face only for a moment—a flash of jaw, an eye, the glint of a blade he held low near her ribs. He told her to give him her phone and her wallet, and she did. He was gone in under a minute. She stood in the alley, shaking, and then she walked to the station and took the train home. She told her husband, and she filed a police report the next morning. The man was never caught.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani found that the memory of that minute did not behave like a normal memory. When it came back—and it came back many times a day—she could taste the metal of the train station railing she had leaned against afterward, or the stale coffee she had drunk at her desk that afternoon. The taste was so sharp and specific that it pulled her back into the alley as if she were still there. Worse, her body would lock into the same position it had been in when the man grabbed her: her right arm slightly raised, her shoulders hunched forward, her breath caught mid-inhale. She would find herself frozen like that on the subway, or at her desk, or in the grocery store aisle, unable to move until the wave passed. And when the wave passed, she often thought, *This cannot have happened to me.* The memory felt too extreme, too cinematic, to belong to her own life.

Leilani began to change how she moved through the world. She stopped wearing headphones outside. She walked home from the train station a different way each night, taking longer routes to avoid the alley, but she could not avoid footsteps. Footsteps behind her, or even nearby, made her heart slam against her ribs. She would stop walking and turn around, or she would duck into a store until the person passed. She also began to scan for the offender’s face, even though she knew rationally that he was not likely to appear in her neighborhood. Still, she found herself studying the jawlines of men in hoodies on the platform, and each time she thought she saw him, her stomach dropped. The worst trigger was unexpected touch. Her husband, reaching for her hand under the dinner table, would make her flinch so hard she knocked over her water glass. He learned to announce himself before touching her, and she was grateful, but she was also ashamed.

At work, Leilani found she could not tolerate delays. If a meeting started late, or a file took longer than expected to load, she became convinced that something terrible was happening—that the delay itself was a sign of danger. She could not relax, even at home in her locked apartment, even with her husband beside her. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that the event had happened because of the sort of person she was. She told herself that she had acted carelessly by walking alone, by wearing headphones, by not looking over her shoulder. She ruminated for hours about how she could have prevented it—if she had left work earlier, if she had taken a different street, if she had screamed. She deliberately tried to leave her body when the memories came, blanking out in front of her computer screen, and she dwelled on what she had done wrong, turning the event over and over in her mind as if she could find the mistake that would undo it.

The consequences accumulated. Her husband asked her to go out for dinner, and she said no because the restaurant was near the alley. Her boss noticed she was taking longer to complete tasks, because she was freezing at her desk or losing time to dissociation. She stopped going to the gym because the locker room was full of sudden touches and unexpected footsteps. She became isolated, and she began to believe that no one could keep her safe, not even the people who told her she was safe now.

What finally brought Leilani to therapy was a morning in late December. She was standing in her kitchen, making coffee, when her husband came up behind her and touched her shoulder to say good morning. She spun around, dropped the mug, and screamed. The mug shattered on the tile. She stood there, shaking, and she thought, *I cannot live like this anymore.* She came to the first session hoping for relief, but what she was most afraid of was that the therapist would tell her she was right—that the world was dangerous, and that she could never feel safe again.
